section.title: Words, Friends, and Folly
section.sectionRationale: Another chapter of independent sentence proverbs from the first Solomonic collection, 10:1 to 22:16. Chapter 18 gathers sayings about isolation and community, the power of the tongue for ruin or refuge, and the difference between many shallow companions and the one friend who sticks closer than a brother.
section.thesis: Life and death are in the power of the tongue, and the isolated, opinionated fool ruins himself, while the humble who seek understanding, trust the LORD as a strong tower, and hold fast to a true friend find safety and life.
section.frameNote: Five clusters: the isolated fool and the fool's mouth; the tongue's power and the strong tower of the LORD's name; hearing before answering; the gift, the wealth, and the wife the LORD gives; the tongue that gives life or death, and the friend who sticks closer than a brother.

verses.text: He who isolates himself pursues selfish desires; he rebels against all sound judgment.
A fool does not delight in understanding, but only in airing his opinions.
With a wicked man comes contempt as well, and shame is accompanied by disgrace.
The words of a man's mouth are deep waters; the fountain of wisdom is a bubbling brook.

units.label: The tongue's power and the LORD's name
units.note: life and death in the mouth

verses.text: Showing partiality to the wicked is not good, nor is depriving the innocent of justice.
A fool's lips bring him strife, and his mouth invites a beating.
A fool's mouth is his ruin, and his lips are a snare to his soul.
The words of a gossip are like choice morsels that go down into the inmost being.
Whoever is slothful in his work is brother to him who destroys.
The name of the LORD is a {{migdal|strong tower}}; the righteous run to it and are safe.
A rich man's wealth is his fortified city; it is like a high wall in his imagination.
Before his downfall a man's heart is proud, but humility comes before honor.
He who answers a matter before he hears it, this is folly and disgrace to him.
The spirit of a man can endure his sickness, but who can survive a broken spirit?
The heart of the discerning acquires knowledge, and the ear of the wise seeks it out.

units.label: Gifts, quarrels, and the wife the LORD gives
units.note: the good things a man finds

verses.text: A man's gift opens doors for him, and brings him before great men.
The first to state his case seems right until another comes and cross-examines him.
Casting the lot ends quarrels and separates strong opponents.
An offended brother is harder to win than a fortified city, and disputes are like the bars of a castle.
From the fruit of his mouth a man's belly is filled; with the harvest from his lips he is satisfied.
Life and death are in the power of the {{lashon|tongue}}, and those who love it will eat its fruit.
He who finds a wife finds a good thing and obtains favor from the LORD.

units.label: A friend closer than a brother
units.note: the poor plead, the rich answer harshly

verses.text: The poor man pleads for mercy, but the rich man answers harshly.
A man of many companions may come to ruin, but there is a {{ohev|friend}} who stays closer than a brother.

migdal.gloss: Strong tower, a fortified place of refuge. Verse 10 names the LORD's own name as this tower, meaning His revealed character and presence, not a magic word, is where the righteous run and find real safety.

lashon.gloss: Tongue, the organ of speech and, by extension, speech itself. Verse 21 says life and death are in its power, a sober claim that words build up or tear down with almost physical force, and that the speaker will eat the fruit of what the tongue produces.

ohev.gloss: One who loves, a loving friend. Verse 24 sets this steady, loving friend against a crowd of many companions who may not endure, describing a bond closer than blood family, one Scripture ultimately locates in Christ.

basic.context: Chapter 18 gathers proverbs about isolation, speech, and friendship. It opens by warning against the man who cuts himself off to chase his own opinions, moves through the terrifying power of the tongue for both ruin and refuge, and ends with the tender claim that some friends love more faithfully than family.
basic.hermeneutics: These are wisdom generalizations, true patterns of how life usually works, not iron laws. Not every isolated person is a fool and not every rich man is safe, but the proverbs press readers to notice how pride, isolation, and a careless tongue tend toward ruin, while humility, community, and careful speech tend toward safety.
basic.originalLanguages: The LORD's name is a migdal, a strong tower, verse 10, where the righteous find real refuge, not a magic charm. The lashon, the tongue, verse 21, holds life and death, a vivid Hebrew way of saying speech has almost physical consequence. And the ohev, the one who loves, verse 24, describes a friend more constant than a blood brother.
basic.typology: The strong tower of the LORD's name, verse 10, anticipates Christ, in whose name alone there is salvation, Acts 4:12. The friend who sticks closer than a brother, verse 24, foreshadows Jesus, who calls His people friends and never abandons them, even to death.
basic.christ: Christ is the name that is now the strong tower into which the righteous run, since salvation is found in no other name, Acts 4:12, and He is the friend who sticks closer than a brother, laying down His life for those He loves, John 15:13. Where chapter 18 warns that the tongue holds life and death, verse 21, the Word made flesh speaks only life, and by His words the dead are raised.
basic.god: God's own name is the place of safety, verse 10, a claim about His character, not a formula; He is trustworthy, and those who run to Him in truth are kept safe. He hates partiality in judgment, verse 5, showing that His justice reaches into the smallest human courtroom disputes as much as the grandest questions of eternity.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 4:12 declares salvation in no other name, echoing the strong tower of 18:10. James 3:1 to 12 develops the tongue's power for blessing and cursing. John 15:13 to 15 names Jesus as the friend who lays down His life. Proverbs 27:6 pairs with 18:24 to distinguish faithful wounds from false flattery.
basic.oneStory: Proverbs 18 warns against isolation, pride, and a reckless tongue, and commends humility, careful listening, and a friend who loves at all times. The whole Bible answers with Jesus, the name that is our strong tower and the friend who sticks closer than a brother, whose words alone hold the power of life.

context.literary:
Proverbs 18 is organised around two images of enclosure, and they pull in opposite directions. The first is the closed self. Verse 1 opens on the man who cuts himself off, verse 2 on the fool who prefers his own opinion to understanding, and the chapter spends many verses on what a mouth can do once nobody else is allowed to answer it. The second image is the fortress. The name of the LORD is a strong tower in verse 10, the rich man's wealth is a fortified city in verse 11, and the wronged brother is harder to win than a fortified city in verse 19. In three verses the same picture of a place of safety is used, once for the LORD, once for money and once for a grievance, so the chapter asks where a person is trying to be safe.

Verses 10 and 11 are set side by side with a deliberate difference. The righteous 'run' to the tower and are 'safe,' while the rich man's wall is high only 'in his imagination.' The chapter then moves into a run of sayings about hearing, with the proud heart and the humble in verse 12, the man who answers before he hears in verse 13, the heart and ear of the discerning in verse 15 and the first witness who seems right until he is questioned in verse 17.

The speech sayings come in two clusters. Verses 4 to 8 move from deep water to the fool's snare and the gossip's morsels, and verses 20 and 21 give the chapter's thesis on the tongue as a source of food and of life or death. The close turns toward people, with the wife who is a gift in verse 22, the poor man who pleads in verse 23, and the friend who clings in verse 24. The chapter is bracketed by the loner at the start and the friend at the end, so that it describes a move from isolation to companionship.
context.historical:
The closed-off man of verse 1 would have been a recognisable figure in Israelite society, which was built on clan, village and family. A person's safety depended on belonging to a household and a community that would defend him, so a man who chose to isolate himself and pursue his own appetites was breaking away from the structure that kept him alive. The wisdom teachers treated that as folly and not as freedom.

Verses 10 and 11 draw on the architecture of walled towns. Cities had towers and gates, and a tower was the last place of retreat in an attack, as in the story of Abimelech, where the people of Thebez fled to the strong tower in the city, Judges 9:51. The 'name of the LORD' meant more than a title. In the Old Testament a name carried the person's character and reputation, and the LORD proclaimed His name to Moses together with His compassion and faithfulness, Exodus 34:5-7. To run to His name was to flee to Him as He is.

Verses 13 and 17 describe how courts worked. A case was heard at the gate, and a hasty judge or a persuasive first speaker could mislead. Moses insisted that judges hear the cases fairly, Deuteronomy 1:16-17. The lot of verse 18 was a recognised way to settle disputes over land and shares, Numbers 26:55. The gift of verse 16 may be a present given to open the way to a powerful man, or a talent that gains an audience, and the warnings against partiality in verse 5 and against bribes elsewhere in the book show that either reading carries a risk. Verse 23 reflects a society where the poor depended on the rich for credit and work.
context.canonical:
Verse 10 is the center of a wide biblical theme of God as a refuge. The psalmist calls Him a rock, a fortress and a stronghold, Psalm 18:2, and a tower of strength against the enemy, Psalm 61:3. He says that some trust in chariots and horses while 'we trust in the name of the LORD our God,' Psalm 20:7. The cities of refuge, to which a person could flee from the avenger, Numbers 35:11-12, are an earlier form of the same idea. In the New Testament Joel's promise that everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved, Joel 2:32, is applied to Jesus by Paul, Romans 10:13, and Peter says salvation is in no other name, Acts 4:12.

Verse 11 is answered by Jesus' parable of the rich man who built larger barns, Luke 12:16-21, and by Paul's instruction not to put hope in the uncertainty of wealth, 1 Timothy 6:17. Verse 12 is nearly word for word the second half of Proverbs 15:33, and the same law is taught again in Luke 14:11.

Verse 13 is echoed in James's advice to be quick to listen and slow to speak, James 1:19, and in Nicodemus's question about whether the law convicts a man without hearing him first, John 7:51. Verse 21 stands behind Jesus' warning that people will give account for every careless word, Matthew 12:36-37, and James 3 on the tongue. Verse 22 recalls Genesis 2:18 and is paired with Proverbs 19:14, and verse 24 is taken up by Jesus' words in John 15:15 and by the promise of Hebrews 13:5-6 that God will never leave or forsake His people.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The sage wanted his hearers to see that wisdom is not a private possession. A person who withdraws to pursue his own desires, who prefers airing his views to understanding, and who answers before he has listened, has chosen a way of life that destroys him. The remedy is humility, the readiness to be questioned, and a circle of people who can say what is true.

He also wanted them to know where to find safety. Wealth feels like a fortified city, and in the imagination it is a high wall, but only the name of the LORD actually protects. The first hearers were meant to compare the two towers and to choose between them, and to run, not drift, to the right one.

And he wanted them to take speech seriously. The mouth feeds the person, verse 20, and the tongue holds life and death, verse 21. He did not offer this as a rule about slips of the tongue but as a description of how words shape a person's world, how they wound and how they heal. The close of the chapter then turns that into a call to love well: receive a wife as a gift of the LORD, answer the poor with mercy, and be the kind of friend who stays.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Some verses here are plainly prescriptive by implication. Run to the name of the LORD, verse 10. Hear before you answer, verse 13. Do not show partiality, verse 5. Choose your words with the knowledge that they bear fruit, verse 21. Others describe. Verse 11 does not say that wealth is wrong, only that it is an imagined wall. Verse 16 says a gift opens doors, which is how things often go, not an endorsement of buying influence. Verse 18 says the lot ends quarrels, and it does not make casting lots the way to settle every dispute today.

Verse 1 should not be read as condemning all solitude. Jesus often withdrew to pray, Luke 5:16, and the verse concerns the man who isolates himself in order to follow his own desires and resist counsel. Verse 22 describes the good of finding a wife and does not command marriage, and Paul commends singleness for some, 1 Corinthians 7. Verse 24's friend is a standard for friendship, not a guarantee that every believer will have one, though the Church is called to be that community, Hebrews 10:24-25.

debates.question: Is verse 22, 'he who finds a wife finds a good thing,' a promise that marriage guarantees blessing?

views.label: A near-universal promise of blessing in marriage
views.case: The verse's positive, unqualified tone can be read as commending marriage itself as an unmixed good and a mark of divine favor.

views.label: A general wisdom observation, not an unconditional guarantee
views.case: Like other Proverbs sayings, it observes a common pattern, a good marriage is a genuine gift from the LORD, without promising that every marriage or every finding of a spouse is trouble free; Proverbs elsewhere, 21:9 and 19, acknowledges painful marriages exist.

debates.bearing: Read as general wisdom rather than unconditional guarantee, the proverb still honors marriage as a genuine good from the LORD while leaving room for the real hardships Proverbs elsewhere names.

debates.question: Does the name of the LORD as a strong tower in verse 10 promise that the righteous will be kept from harm?

views.label: Yes, the righteous are kept safe from harm in this life
views.case: The verse says the righteous run to the tower 'and are safe.' Psalm 91:2 and Proverbs 14:26 speak of the LORD as a refuge and a place of confidence, and the plain sense of the proverb seems to be that those who trust Him will not be overcome.

views.label: No, the safety is spiritual and final, and it does not mean the absence of suffering
views.case: Hebrews 11:36-38 lists believers who were mocked, flogged, imprisoned and put to death, and the world was not worthy of them. Jesus tells His followers that in the world they will have tribulation, and also that He has overcome it, John 16:33. The tower protects the person, but it does not always prevent injury.

debates.bearing: Proverbs gives patterns, not guarantees, and the second view fits the whole Bible. The name of the LORD is a real and sufficient refuge, and what it secures is the believer's standing with God and his ultimate end. That is a safety that suffering, even martyrdom, cannot touch, and it is the reason the righteous can run to it in trouble.

debates.question: How should the difficult first line of verse 24 be read?

views.label: Many companions may bring a man to ruin
views.case: The BSB follows this reading, taking the verb as 'be broken' or 'come to ruin.' It sets a crowd of casual friends against the one friend who stays, and warns that quantity is no substitute for loyalty. It fits Proverbs 19:4, which shows how fair-weather friends fall away.

views.label: A man with friends must show himself friendly
views.case: The older English tradition reads the verb as 'to show oneself a friend,' which gives the sense that friendship is earned by being friendly. Other versions render it so that some friends only pretend to friendship.

debates.bearing: Every reading agrees on the second line, that there is a friend who clings closer than a brother. The first line is a question of translation, and the BSB reading carries the sharpest contrast. Wherever the verb lands, the proverb tells the reader to value a few steady friends above a crowd and to be one.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1's isolated man 'pursues selfish desires,' and the noun is ta'avah, craving, the same root as the cry for meat in the wilderness and the longing of the wicked in other proverbs. What he rebels against is tushiyyah, translated 'sound judgment,' a word for wisdom that works in practice, as in Proverbs 3:21. The man is not merely alone. He is against what actually succeeds.

Verse 2 says the fool delights in 'airing his opinions.' Literally it is 'uncovering his heart,' lehitgalot libbo. The fool is an exhibitionist of the mind, who takes pleasure in laying out what he thinks. Verse 4 then offers a contrast with water. 'Deep waters,' mayim amuqqim, is the image used in Proverbs 20:5 for the purposes of the heart, which the man of understanding draws out. Words rise from a depth, and what a person says reveals what is down there.

Verse 5's 'showing partiality' is literally 'lifting the face,' se'et panim, as the BSB footnote notes. It is the courtroom idiom for favoritism, where the judge looks up at the face of the powerful and favors him, and Leviticus 19:15 forbids it. In verse 8 the gossip's words go down to the 'inmost being,' chadrei-beten, literally the chambers of the belly. The same phrase appears in Proverbs 20:27, where the LORD's lamp searches those chambers, so what gossip reaches, God's light also reaches. Verse 8 is repeated in Proverbs 26:22.

In verse 10 the righteous are 'safe,' nisgav, a verb that means to be set high, beyond reach, and the same verb appears in Proverbs 29:25: whoever trusts in the LORD is set securely on high. Safety is a height. Verse 11's wealth is a high wall 'in his imagination,' and the Hebrew noun, maskit, can mean a carved or figured thing. Psalm 73:7 uses its plural for the imaginations of the proud heart. The rich man's wall is a picture he has made and keeps looking at.

Verse 13 says the one who answers 'before he hears,' and the verb means to return a word. The foolish response is a reply sent back before the message arrived. In verse 17 the neighbor 'cross-examines,' from the root chaqar, to search and probe, the verb of Proverbs 25:2, where kings search out a matter. Verse 21 says that life and death are 'in the power of the tongue,' and the Hebrew is literally 'in the hand of the tongue,' beyad lashon, as though the tongue held life and death in its grip.

In verse 24 the friend 'stays closer than a brother,' and the verb is dabeq, to cling. It is the verb used for a man being united to his wife, Genesis 2:24, for Ruth clinging to Naomi, Ruth 1:14, and for Israel holding fast to the LORD, Deuteronomy 10:20. It is covenant vocabulary applied to a friendship.

typology.type: The strong tower and the city of refuge, verse 10
typology.fulfillment: Israel had actual places to run to: the cities of refuge where a person who had killed without intent could flee from the avenger and stand trial, Numbers 35:11-12. The author of Hebrews uses that picture of believers who have 'fled to take hold of the hope set before us,' Hebrews 6:18. The name that gives safety is now the name of Jesus, at which every knee will bow, Philippians 2:9-10, and no other name saves, Acts 4:12. The type falls short because a city of refuge could protect only a person who had not murdered, and only within its walls, while Christ shelters sinners and goes with them.

typology.type: The friend who clings closer than a brother, verse 24
typology.fulfillment: Jonathan, Ruth and Moses, whom the LORD addressed as a friend, are faint preparations for the friendship Jesus offers. He says to His disciples, 'I have called you friends,' because He has made known to them all He heard from the Father, John 15:15. The promise of Hebrews 13:5-6 that God will never leave or forsake His people is the clinging of verse 24 with the weight of divine faithfulness. The type is exceeded in what Christ does as a friend. He does not merely stay near in trouble but goes into death in the place of His friends, and rises.

typology.type: The tongue that holds life and death, verse 21
typology.fulfillment: The proverb has the tongue in whose grip life and death lie. Jesus is the one in whom this is literally true. He says that the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God and those who hear will live, John 5:25. At the tomb of Lazarus He calls in a loud voice, 'Lazarus, come out!' and the dead man comes out, John 11:43-44. Isaiah's servant has been given 'the tongue of discipleship, to sustain the weary with a word,' Isaiah 50:4. The correspondence is complete in a way no human speaker can match. Human words can wound or encourage, but only His word gives life that death cannot reverse.

typology.type: The wife found as a gift, verse 22
typology.fulfillment: The verse echoes Genesis 2, where it was 'not good' for the man to be alone and the LORD brought him a wife, Genesis 2:18. Paul takes marriage as a picture of Christ and the church, a mystery he calls profound, Ephesians 5:32, and the Lord says He came to seek and save the lost, Luke 19:10. Christ is the bridegroom who finds His people and gives Himself up for them, Ephesians 5:25. The type has a limit: Proverbs speaks of a man finding good, but in the gospel the Bridegroom finds a bride who has nothing to give and makes her good.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first as the name that is a tower. Joel promised that everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved, Joel 2:32, and Paul applies that promise to the Lord Jesus, Romans 10:13. At the name of Jesus every knee will bow, Philippians 2:9-10, and Peter says salvation is in no other name, Acts 4:12. That the name of the LORD, in this chapter, is the safe place, and that the New Testament places Jesus in the center of that name, is one of the plainest lines from the book of Proverbs to the person of Christ. It is not an allegorical stretch. The New Testament itself uses the 'name of the LORD' language for Him.

It leads to Christ as the Word whose speech gives life. Verse 21 gives the tongue the power of life and death. John begins by calling Jesus the Word who was with God and was God, John 1:1, who became flesh, John 1:14. He answered the tempter with the word of God, Matthew 4:4, He stilled a storm with a command, Mark 4:39, and He called a dead man out of a grave, John 11:43-44. Isaiah's servant speaks to sustain the weary, Isaiah 50:4, and the Gospels show Jesus answering the blind beggar by first stopping and asking, 'What do you want Me to do for you?' Luke 18:40-41. That is the hearing before answering of verse 13, and the opposite of the rich man's harsh reply in verse 23.

It leads to Christ as the friend. Verse 24 speaks of the friend who clings, and the Gospels show Him as the friend of sinners. He wept at the tomb of a friend, John 11:35, and He promises never to leave or forsake His people, Hebrews 13:5-6. The friendship is not only comfort. It also tells them what He has heard from the Father, John 15:15.

It leads to Christ in the broken spirit of verse 14. The proverb asks who can survive it. Isaiah calls the Servant a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief, Isaiah 53:3, and on the cross Jesus cried, 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?' Matthew 27:46. He bore the one burden no human spirit can bear, and He survived it, in the sense that He rose.

It leads to Christ as the one who warns about the rich man's wall. In Luke 12:16-21 a man trusts in full barns and loses his life that night. Jesus says it is hard for the rich to enter the kingdom, Mark 10:24-25. The only fortress is the one He is.

The caution is not to treat every proverb about the tongue or friendship as a prediction of Christ. They are wisdom for ordinary life, and they come to rest on Him where the New Testament shows the connection.
study.god:
The chapter's central claim about God is that He is a place. The name of the LORD is a strong tower, and the righteous run into it. A name in Hebrew thought was the person's revealed character, and when the LORD proclaimed His name to Moses He listed compassion, grace, patience, loving devotion and faithfulness, Exodus 34:5-7. So the tower is made of these qualities, and running to it means casting oneself on what God has shown Himself to be. It is not a charm. Exodus 20:7 shows how seriously the name is to be taken, and Psalm 20:7 contrasts trust in the name with trust in chariots and horses.

He is impartial. Verse 5 says that it is not good to show partiality to the wicked or to deprive the innocent of justice, and Deuteronomy 10:17 says that the LORD shows no partiality and accepts no bribe. The standard set for human judges is a mirror of His own character. The poor man who pleads in verse 23 and gets a harsh answer from the rich has a God who hears. In Exodus 3:7 He says, 'I have heard them crying out.'

He is the giver of good gifts in ordinary life. Verse 22 says that the one who finds a wife obtains favor from the LORD, and Proverbs 19:14 adds that a prudent wife is from the LORD. Marriage is not dismissed as a mere social arrangement. God stands behind it as a gift.

He holds speech to account. The chapter treats words as having weight, and Jesus says that people will give account for every careless word, Matthew 12:36-37. God made the tongue a thing of life and death, and Deuteronomy 30:19 sets before His people life and death and says to choose life.

He is a friend. Verse 24 is not about God directly, but the Bible calls Abraham God's friend, James 2:23, and says that He spoke to Moses as to a friend, Exodus 33:11. The God who is a tower is also a companion.

There is a tension in the chapter. The tower is safe, and yet God allows the righteous to suffer. Hebrews 11 tells of people who were mistreated and for whom the world was not worthy. The Bible does not resolve this by denying either side. The tower is real, and the safety it gives is deeper than the avoidance of harm.

For worship, this chapter invites a person to run, which is an act of the whole will. Prayer in trouble is the running, and praise is what remains when one has arrived and found the door open.

crossReferences.note: The intentions of a man's heart are deep waters, but a man of understanding draws them out. It extends verse 4's image: what comes out of the mouth rises from depths, and wisdom is the skill of drawing it up gently, by questions, instead of leaving the fool to pour out whatever he has.

David calls God his refuge, a tower of strength against the enemy. It is the same picture as verse 10, set in a prayer from a man who was in flight and needed the tower he describes. It confirms that the strong tower is a place found in experience, by people under pressure.

Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but 'we trust in the name of the LORD our God.' The psalm sets the name against the military power of the age, as the proverb sets it against wealth. Both teach that the name of the LORD is a different kind of security from anything a person can build.

Jesus tells of a rich man who stored up his crops, built larger barns and said to himself to relax, and God called him a fool because his life was demanded that night. It is verse 11 acted out: the high wall of wealth stood only in his imagination.

Nicodemus asks the other leaders whether the law convicts a man without first hearing from him. He appeals to the same principle as verse 13, that to judge before hearing is folly, and the objection of a single careful man briefly stopped a rush to condemn Jesus.

James tells believers to be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to anger. It is the proverb's wisdom about answering put as a three part habit. The order matters: hearing comes first, speech second, and anger last.

Jesus says people will give an account on the day of judgment for every careless word, and by their words they will be acquitted or condemned. This takes verse 21's life and death in the tongue to its ultimate setting, the final reckoning.

The LORD says it is not good for the man to be alone. Verse 22 calls the wife 'a good thing,' and the echo is deliberate: the proverb sees marriage as part of God's answer to the first thing in creation He called not good.

Orpah kisses her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clings to her. The verb is the one in verse 24 for the friend who stays closer than a brother. Ruth's loyalty, given to a family not her own and at great cost, is the best narrative picture of the friend the proverb describes.

God has said, 'Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you,' so we say with confidence that the Lord is our helper. It gives the friend of verse 24 a divine anchor: the promise of a companion who will not leave belongs to those who trust Him.

The Servant has been given the tongue of a disciple, to sustain the weary with a word, and He listens each morning. Hearing precedes speaking, and so the Servant embodies both halves of the chapter: the listening ear of verse 15 and the life-giving tongue of verse 21.

At Babel the people say, 'let us build for ourselves a city with a tower,' to make a name for themselves. The Hebrew word for tower is the one in verse 10. The people build a tower for their own name, while the proverb says the only tower that keeps anyone safe is the name of the LORD.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with one man alone in a good garden, and the LORD says it is not good, Genesis 2:18. Everything in Proverbs 18 about isolation and companionship starts there. The first human words after the fall are an exercise in hiding and blaming, and the first great human project is a city with a tower. At Babel the people want a name for themselves and a place that cannot be scattered, Genesis 11:4, and the word for their tower is the one Proverbs 18:10 uses for the strong tower of the LORD's name. The chapter sets the two side by side: a tower built to make a name, and a name that is itself the tower.

The LORD answers Babel by confusing the tongue, Genesis 11:7, and the story of Israel then moves toward the refuge He provides, with cities where the fleeing could find safety, a temple where His name would dwell, and psalms that call Him a rock and a fortress. Fortified cities throughout the story fall: the walls of kings and rich men, and finally Jerusalem. In every case the lesson is that what looked secure was an imagined wall.

The gospel brings the name down into history. Jesus is the Word through whom everything was made, and His word gives life. He is the friend who stays, and He is the one who bears the broken spirit no one else could survive. At Pentecost the flames of fire rest on the believers and they speak in other tongues, Acts 2:3-4, a reversal of Babel in which the tongue becomes again a gift for gathering instead of scattering.

The story ends with the nations before the throne, from every tribe and people and tongue, Revelation 7:9. The name of the LORD is written on His people, Revelation 22:4, so the tower is no longer a place they run to but a mark they bear. They see His face. The solitary man is gone, and the friend who clings closer than a brother is with them, as God Himself dwells among them, Revelation 21:3.

quiz.q: According to verse 1, what happens to the man who isolates himself?

options.text: He pursues selfish desires and rebels against all sound judgment.
options.note: Isolation from community counsel is tied to selfish rebellion against wisdom.

options.text: He becomes wiser through solitude.
options.note: The verse presents isolation negatively, not as a path to wisdom.

options.text: He avoids all conflict successfully.
options.note: The verse's concern is selfish rebellion, not conflict avoidance.

options.text: He gains sound judgment through independence.
options.note: This reverses the verse; isolation is linked to rebelling against sound judgment, not gaining it.

quiz.q: What does verse 10 call the name of the LORD?

options.text: A strong tower where the righteous run and are safe.
options.note: The LORD's revealed name and character are pictured as a fortified refuge.

options.text: A fortified city belonging to the rich.
options.note: That image describes the rich man's wealth in verse 11, a false security by contrast.

options.text: A weapon against enemies.
options.note: The image is refuge, not a weapon.

options.text: A high wall in a man's imagination.
options.note: This phrase describes the rich man's false confidence in verse 11, not the true safety of verse 10.

quiz.q: What does verse 21 say is in the power of the tongue?

options.text: Life and death.
options.note: Speech has weighty, almost physical consequence for good or ill.

options.text: Only death, never life.
options.note: The verse names both life and death as possible fruits of speech.

options.text: Wealth and poverty only.
options.note: The verse's terms are life and death, broader than material wealth.

options.text: Mostly life, with death being rare.
options.note: The verse presents both possibilities without weighting one as rare.

options.text: Answering a matter before hearing it out, calling this folly and disgrace.
options.note: The proverb condemns hasty, premature answers.

options.text: Listening too long before responding.
options.note: This is the opposite of the verse's actual warning.

options.text: Speaking with eloquence.
options.note: The verse's concern is timing and listening, not eloquence.

options.text: Answering quickly but politely.
options.note: Politeness does not address the core problem the verse names, answering before hearing.

quiz.q: How does verse 24 describe a certain kind of friend?

options.text: A friend who stays closer than a brother, unlike many companions who may lead to ruin.
options.note: The verse contrasts shallow, numerous companions with one deeply loyal friend.

options.text: A friend who is useful only when convenient.
options.note: This is the opposite of the loyal, constant friend the verse describes.

options.text: Many companions are always better than one close friend.
options.note: The verse actually warns that many companions may lead to ruin.

options.text: A friend who is somewhat close, similar to an acquaintance.
options.note: The verse's language is much stronger, closer than a brother, not merely acquaintance level.

questions: Verse 1 warns against isolating yourself to chase your own opinions. Where might you be cutting yourself off from wise counsel right now?
The tongue holds life and death, verse 21. What is one recent conversation where your words gave life, and one where they may have brought harm?
The LORD's name is a strong tower, verse 10. What are you running to for safety instead of Him this season, wealth, reputation, control?
Verse 13 warns against answering before listening. Who in your life deserves a slower, more attentive hearing from you?
Verse 24 names a friend who stays closer than a brother. Are you cultivating that kind of costly, constant friendship, or settling for many shallow companions?

translationNotes.note: 'Strong tower' translates migdal oz, a fortified tower; the phrase pictures the LORD's revealed name, His character and covenant promises, as a literal refuge, not a magic incantation.
The Hebrew places 'death and life' before 'tongue,' emphasizing the weight of the claim; some translations reorder for English flow, as BSB does here with 'life and death.'

The Hebrew behind 'a man of many companions' can also suggest 'a man who has friends must show himself friendly,' a reading some older translations follow, though the sense of contrast with the one loyal friend remains the same.
